cf.title: Support casts from numeric to oid8

input.subject: [PATCH] Support casts from numeric to oid8

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection stops the idea at level 1 or 2. already-exists-1 asks for demand, but the cost is one pg_cast row and one function, and the cast mirrors the existing numeric-to-int8 cast. standards-compat-1 is a fixable design point: the proposal gives no reason for accepting negatives down to -18446744073709551615 in assignment context. Only one message is visible, so the list's view of the wraparound rule is unknown.

brief.title: Add an assignment cast from numeric to oid8
brief.problem: Integer literals above INT64_MAX parse as numeric, and there is no numeric-to-oid8 cast, so `SELECT 18446744073709551615::oid8` fails although the value fits in oid8. The quoted form '18446744073709551615'::oid8 works. Users who write large oid8 values as plain literals hit this error.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a numeric-to-oid8 cast usable in assignment and explicit contexts only. It rounds to the nearest integer with ties away from zero, requires the rounded magnitude to fit in uint64, and wraps negative results modulo 2^64 like oid8 text input. NaN and infinity are rejected, with soft-error support.
user_visible_surface: New pg_cast entry: numeric to oid8, assignment context.
New conversion function in pg_proc backing the cast; the material does not give its name.
Documentation paragraph in datatype.sgml on numeric-to-oid8 rounding, range and wraparound.
Negative numeric values convert by wraparound, for example -1 becomes 18446744073709551615.
author_claims: Numeric can represent every oid8 value exactly, while signed integer types cannot represent the upper half of the range.
An implicit cast would round fractional values in comparisons, so `2::oid8 = 1.5` would return true.
Wrapping negative numeric input matches earlier discussion that negative oid8 text input wraps on purpose.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. No one has replied.
unclear: The patch does not say whether a matching oid8-to-numeric cast exists or is needed.
The proposal does not justify rounding fractional input instead of rejecting it, as text input would.
The material does not say whether similar casts for oid, or for other integer types to oid8, are in scope.
The proposal does not say why the absolute-value bound allows negative values down to -18446744073709551615, which wrap to small positive values.
search_queries: large integer literal parsed as numeric

objections.title: Quoted literal already covers the full oid8 range
objections.failure_scenario: A user who writes 18446744073709551615::oid8 gets an error today. Writing '18446744073709551615'::oid8, or value::text::oid8 for a computed numeric, already gives the result. The patch adds a permanent pg_cast and pg_proc entry so that the quotes can be dropped.
objections.argument: Message #1 states that the quoted form works, so the existing way can do the job with two extra characters. For computed numeric values, a cast through text reaches the existing oid8 input function. Message #1 shows no field report or user request, and oid8 values above INT64_MAX are rare in practice. A committer would likely ask whether this convenience justifies a new catalog cast that must be kept forever.
objections.author_must_show: Which users or tools write oid8 values above INT64_MAX as bare literals or numeric expressions, and why does quoting or casting through text not work for them?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 itself shows the quoted form works, and the thread shows no user report or reply. The cost is small and falls on few people, so this is a request to show demand and does not count against the design.

objections.title: Assignment cast wraps negative numeric values into large oid8 values
objections.failure_scenario: An application inserts a computed numeric such as -1.0 or -18446744073709551615 into an oid8 column. The row silently stores 18446744073709551615 or 1 instead of raising an error. The user finds out later, when lookups by that identifier return the wrong object or nothing.
objections.argument: The cast applies in assignment context, so INSERT and UPDATE take this path without any explicit request. Message #1 justifies the wraparound by pointing to oid8 text input, but text input is a compatibility rule for strings, and a cast from an arithmetic type is a different contract. The doc context the patch extends already shows `INSERT INTO mytable VALUES(-1);  -- fails` for the OID types, so -1 would fail while -1.0 succeeds. The bound on the absolute value also accepts negatives that wrap to small positive values, which look valid.
objections.author_must_show: Why should an assignment cast from numeric wrap negative values instead of raising "out of range" as the other integer-to-OID conversions do?

critic.reasoning: The proposal gives no reason for accepting values down to -18446744073709551615, which wrap to small positive values in assignment. The cited `VALUES(-1); -- fails` line is hunk context that looks like the domain example, and int4-to-oid already wraps, so neither supports the objection.

refuted.title: Assignment cast commits oid8 to silent rounding and wraparound
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs `insert into t (ref) select n from staging` with an oid8 column `ref`. A staging value of 41.5 is stored as 42, and -1 is stored as 18446744073709551615, with no error. Both look like valid identifiers, so the bad reference shows up only when a lookup returns the wrong object or no object.
refuted.argument: oid8 holds identifiers, where a nearby value names a different object, but the patch rounds fractional numeric input, while text input rejects fractions. Because the cast is an assignment cast, INSERT and UPDATE apply it without any explicit `::oid8`. Once released, applications may depend on this behaviour, so changing it later to reject fractions would break them. Message #1 justifies wraparound by pointing to text input, but gives no reason for rounding, which text input does not do.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should a fractional or negative numeric be accepted silently in assignment to an identifier type, instead of raising an error as non-integral text input does?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the wraparound part. The rounding part copies existing practice: numeric-to-int8 is also an assignment cast that rounds ties away from zero, while int8 text input rejects fractions.

refuted.title: New cast path has different rules from oid8 text input
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs insert into t values (1.5) into an oid8 column and stores 2 without any error, while '1.5'::oid8 and 1.5::text::oid8 are rejected. The two paths to oid8 disagree, and the user learns of the silent rounding only when the stored values do not match the source data.
refuted.argument: The commit message rounds fractional numeric with ties away from zero. The oid8 text input, which the brief says is the model for wraparound, does not accept fractions. So the patch adds a second way into oid8 that follows the text input for negative values but not for fractions. It also accepts values down to -18446744073709551615, which wrap to small positive OIDs, and the proposal gives no reason for this.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should the numeric cast round fractional values and accept large negative values when the existing text input path, which the patch claims to follow, rejects fractions?

critic.reasoning: The same difference exists today for int8: `1.5::int8` rounds to 2 in assignment, and `'1.5'::int8` is rejected. So the patch follows existing numeric-to-integer practice. The large-negative part is a duplicate of standards-compat-1.

refuted.title: No user report for unquoted oid8 literals above INT64_MAX
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes 18446744073709551615::oid8 and gets an error, then quotes the literal and it works. The patch adds a permanent pg_cast entry with rounding and wraparound rules to save that one edit. Everyone who reads pg_cast and the datatype docs carries the new rules.
refuted.argument: Message #1 starts from a question asked out of curiosity and cites no field report, -general or -bugs thread, or application that hit the error. It also shows the workaround: '18446744073709551615'::oid8 already works. Generated oid8 values come from counters that start low, so literals above INT64_MAX are rare outside tests and hand-written edge cases. The cast also adds behaviour, rounding 1.5 and wrapping -1, that someone must document and defend later.
refuted.author_must_show: Which applications or tools write unquoted oid8 literals above INT64_MAX, or assign numeric values to oid8 columns, and what do they do today?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which states the same demand question and also covers computed numeric values through text. The claim that message #1 was asked out of curiosity is not supported by the material.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: The patch adds one pg_cast row and one pg_proc row for the numeric-to-oid8 conversion.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The new assignment cast rounds fractional numeric input and wraps negative values modulo 2^64 without an error.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The rounding and wraparound rules of the cast become behaviour that applications can depend on after release.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #1 states that the quoted form '18446744073709551615'::oid8 already works.

questions: Why does the cast accept negative numeric values down to -18446744073709551615 in assignment context, where they wrap to small positive oid8 values, instead of raising an out-of-range error?
Which users or tools write oid8 values above INT64_MAX as unquoted literals or numeric expressions, and why does quoting or a cast through text not work for them?
Does an oid8-to-numeric cast exist, and if not, should this patch add it so the conversion has both directions?
Are matching casts for oid, or from other integer types to oid8, in scope for this work?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows the numeric code and the oid8 type would have to own it; nobody has replied to message #1.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the cast's rounding, range and wraparound rules for as long as oid8 exists, because applications can come to depend on them after release.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way; message #1 ends with "Comments welcome".

priority.reason: The patch is about 7.5 KiB, touches numeric.c and two catalog data files, and helps only users who write oid8 values above INT64_MAX as numeric. The negative-range rule should be settled on the list before commit.

provisional_note: Without the code, the range check, the soft-error path and the volatility and leakproof marking of the new function could not be checked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Precision loss casting float to numeric
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Robert Haas, Bear Giles
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the float4 and float8 to numeric casts keep full binary precision, so that the cast and the round trip back to float no longer lose bits. The proof-of-concept patch printed values with FLT_DECIMAL_DIG and DBL_DECIMAL_DIG digits in place of FLT_DIG and DBL_DIG, and the author planned a frexp-based conversion.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane and Robert Haas expected more complaints about results such as 1.1::float8 casting to an odd-looking numeric than benefit from exact values, and Bear Giles asked that existing results not change. Making the cast follow extra_float_digits would make it stable instead of immutable. Per-schema casts cannot work because casts have no names, which left a separate named function as the remaining option. The author marked the entry Returned with feedback, citing the backward-compatibility issues and lack of time in this CF.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think there's probably a bigger chance of complaints that "casting 1.1::float8 to numeric now produces some weird, incorrectly-rounded result" than that we make anyone happier.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add numeric_trim(numeric)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Dean Rasheed, Alvaro Herrera, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a function numeric_trim(numeric) that removes trailing zeros after the decimal point by lowering the value's display scale. Reviewers also discussed a minscale() function that returns the smallest scale needed, to be used with round().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed found a bug: numeric_trim(1e100) fails with "value overflows numeric format" because the computed dscale goes negative. He also asked for a simpler implementation based on strip_var(), and the thread moved toward a minscale() design. The author did not post a new version, so Alvaro Herrera and later Robert Haas closed the entry as returned with feedback.
matched_queries: large integer literal parsed as numeric
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think this patch got useful feedback but we never saw a followup
version posted.  I closed it as returned-with-feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: remove single character literal tokens from the core grammar
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace all single character literal tokens in the core, PL/pgSQL and ECPG grammars with named tokens, so the grammar can later use Bison 3.5's "%define api.token.raw" and skip the yytranslate[] lookup. The author measured about 1.7-1.9% faster raw parsing with the option enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that the patch only moves the character-to-token mapping from the parser into the lexer, so it may not be an improvement. He also judged the patch too invasive for a small gain that needs Bison 3.5, a version the project would not require for a long time. The visible messages show no further discussion before the rejection.

precedents_retrieved.title: Autoprepare: implicitly replace literals with parameters and store generalized plan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made the server detect queries repeated with different literal values, replace the literals with parameters, and cache a generic plan per session, like an implicit prepared statement. A later version limited this to extended query mode, where it turned unnamed statements into prepared ones.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that the feature would hurt more use cases than it helps. Restricted to extended query mode, it only overrides the application's choice of unnamed statements, which the client can change more easily and with better knowledge. He also noted that the plancache already chooses generic plans wrongly in real workloads, that the pgbench benchmarks showed only best cases with no worst-case or cache-pressure numbers, and that the patch had no tests; the author sent nothing more, so the entry was returned with feedback.
matched_queries: large integer literal parsed as numeric
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that extending that behavior to more cases is going to be a net loss, until we find some way to make it smarter and more reliable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Implicit prepare of statements: replace literals with parameters and store cached plans
precedents_retrieved.summary: When a query with different literal values repeats many times in one backend, replace the literals with parameters and run it as an implicitly prepared statement with a cached plan. The cache is per backend and is controlled by an autoprepare_threshold setting, for clients that cannot use prepared statements, such as connections through pgbouncer.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch moved through several commitfests without review, and the shown messages are about rebases and build fixes only. David Steele returned it with feedback in the final PG11 commitfest because it had no review or comments since May 2017 and he judged it too complex and invasive for that commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: 64-bit XIDs
precedents_retrieved.authors: Aleksander Alekseev (a.alekseev), Pavel Borisov (pborisov), Konstantin Knizhnik (knizhnik), Maxim Orlov (m.orlov), Yura Sokolov (funny_falcon), Fedor Sigaev (sigaev), Alexander Korotkov (smagen), Nikita Glukhov (n.glukhov)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change TransactionId to 64 bits in memory while keeping 32-bit xmin/xmax in heap tuples, storing a 64-bit xid_base and multi_base in each heap page's special space and computing tuple XIDs as offsets from them, with a "double xmax" fallback format for upgraded pages that lack free space. The patch was based on earlier work by Alexander Korotkov and on an implementation used in the Postgres Pro fork.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry as Returned with Feedback because the patch had not applied for some time and the discussion had moved to higher-level design questions without a consensus on how to proceed. Before that, Chris Travers objected that removing wraparound pressure without mitigations, such as a configurable XID-lag warning, could turn freezing and vacuum problems into later and more serious outages. The author side also stated that the thread was waiting for the SLRU-related groundwork patches to be committed first. The work was later resubmitted in a new commitfest entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch hasn't applied in quite some time, and the thread has moved to
discussing higher lever items rather than the suggested patch, so I'm closing
this as Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: 64-bit XIDs
precedents_retrieved.authors: Aleksander Alekseev (a.alekseev), Pavel Borisov (pborisov), Konstantin Knizhnik (knizhnik), Maxim Orlov (m.orlov), Yura Sokolov (funny_falcon), Fedor Sigaev (sigaev), Alexander Korotkov (smagen), Nikita Glukhov (n.glukhov)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes TransactionId 64-bit in memory and keeps 32-bit xmin and xmax on disk as offsets from a per-page xid_base and multi_base stored in the page special space. Pages without room for that special space after pg_upgrade switch to a "double xmax" tuple format until vacuum frees space.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Aleksander Alekseev closed the entry because the thread reached no consensus on switching to 64-bit XIDs, and the patchset was hard to rebase and review. Michael Paquier also asked for a summary, since there was no clear agreement on an epoch:xid to 64-bit XID switch. Chris Travers objected to removing the wraparound safety limits without a replacement warning on XID lag, so autovacuum problems would not stay hidden. Independent parts were split into their own threads: 64-bit GUCs, removing short SLRU file names, and 64-bit MultiXactOffset.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To me it seems like we didn't reach a consensus regarding switching to 64-bit XIDs.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P3] concerns changing the results of the existing float-to-numeric casts, and its reason (complaints about changed, odd-looking results) does not apply to adding a new numeric-to-oid8 cast. Message #1 cites an earlier discussion where negative oid8 text input wraps on purpose, and uses it as support for the design, not as a prior rejection.
Rounding of fractional values follows the existing numeric-to-integer casts, so I raise no objection to it. Keeping the cast out of implicit context avoids changing existing comparisons.

The patch adds one pg_cast row and one pg_proc row, which means a catversion bump and nothing else persistent. It has no on-disk format, WAL, replication, wire protocol or ABI change. The cast is immutable and has no locale or GUC dependence, so standbys and subscribers compute the same result. One edge case is a user-defined numeric-to-oid8 cast in an older cluster, which would conflict during pg_upgrade, but every new built-in cast carries that cost.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds a built-in pg_cast entry and conversion function in assignment and explicit contexts only, so function and operator resolution does not change. Users gain no new data, files or sessions, and the conversion is bounded, so it adds no denial-of-service path. Leakproof marking of the new function cannot be checked without the code, but a function that raises errors would not normally be leakproof.
Apart from the semantics above, the maintenance cost is small: one pg_cast row, one function, no hot-path or extension API impact.
Two objections raised; the listed precedent [P3] is about float-to-numeric precision and does not apply here.
The cost is small and falls mostly on catalog and docs, so the objection is "show demand", not a rejection.
